correctness.rationale: The open-neighborhood process splits by bipartition side. On \(L\), \(N(u)=R\) and \(N(b_i)=\{v,a_i\}\), so any legal \(L\)-subsequence has length at most \(n\): without \(u\) there are only \(n\) choices, while with \(u\), the vertex \(u\) must be last and at most \(n-1\) of the \(b_i\) can precede it. Equality is exactly all \(b_i\) in arbitrary order, or \(n-1\) vertices \(b_i\) in arbitrary order followed by \(u\). The same holds on \(R\). Independent interleaving yields length \(2n\), forces the complement form, and gives \(\binom{2n}{n}(2n!)(2n!)=4(2n)!\) ordered maxima. A direct dynamic-programming checker verifies \(1\le n\le7\) from the definition.

value.rationale: The theorem gives complete witness-level structure for a canonical graph family: every maximum set is described by a two-vertex bipartition complement, and every ordered maximum sequence is counted exactly by \(4(2n)!\). This is materially finer than the scalar Grundy total domination number, provides a natural benchmark for enumeration algorithms, and exposes a reusable side-independence mechanism rather than an arbitrary finite slice.
